turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Sunday, the eighteenth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
[curious] Three things up top. Iran and America both say they control the Strait of Hormuz, and the people who count the ships say they can't.
[curious] A plant that catches ants by making a surface that only works when it's raining.
[thoughtful] And Bernina closed its last Swiss production line in May, while its Singapore website still says Swiss tradition since eighteen ninety-three.
[wry] Start with the strait, because the numbers there are extraordinary.
[wry] Saturday the seventeenth. Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy declares the Strait of Hormuz closed.
[amused] Closed closed? As in, nothing moves?
That's the claim. Within hours the commander of US Central Command, Admiral Brad Cooper, says the opposite — the strait is, quote, controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran.
[skeptical] So two governments, same water, opposite claims. Who's right?
[deadpan] That's the thing. Nobody can say.
[skeptical] Somebody must be counting.

Somebody is. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre publishes a weekly tally. Twelve ships attacked in the week to the sixteenth. Six continued or reached port, two disabled, three unconfirmed, and one lost — a Singapore-flagged container ship, the GFS Pride.
[warmly] One of ours.
[chuckles] One of ours. But here's the line in their own report. They say they are, quote, struggling to accurately report true number of attacks.
[pause] The people whose job is counting say they can't count.
Because most captains never file a report. And it goes further. They logged two hundred and fifty-four transits in a week. Only forty-two of those were actually observed.
[pause] Forty-two out of two hundred and fifty-four. What were the rest?
[exhales] American-reported, quote, facilitated transits, which the centre states plainly it cannot independently verify.
[exhales] So the number everyone's arguing about is mostly unverifiable.

Central Command counts its own way and says roughly four hundred ships went through. Kpler, counting cargoes, puts flows at eleven point six million barrels a day — about sixty-eight per cent of the pre-war baseline.
[curious] Which is neither closed nor open.

Neither closed nor open. The one voice with no side to take is the International Maritime Organization. Its secretary-general says more than a hundred and ten vessels have been hit since February, at least twenty-four seafarers are confirmed dead, and about six thousand are stranded.
[thoughtful] Stranded. On ships.
[wry] His advice now is simply to avoid the strait. He said: we cannot put the lives of innocent seafarers at risk anymore.
[amused] And the oil price?
[skeptical] Brent settled Friday at one hundred and nine dollars eighty-six, up almost five per cent on the week.
[thoughtful] Does the sceptic have anything here?

The sceptic is the American government's own forecaster. The Energy Information Administration, on the sixth of October, forecasts Brent averaging a hundred and five this quarter and falling to eighty-four next year.
Eighty-four. That's a long way below where we are.
And it explicitly assumes convoys and workarounds let regional exports rise. So the official American view is that the strait degrades rather than closes.
What would settle it?

Their own count. Transits only fell from two hundred and seventy-five to two hundred and fifty-four in a record week of attacks. If next week holds above two hundred and fifty while Brent stays over a hundred and ten, the premium is in the price and not in the water.
Right. And there's a second Washington story that ties straight into this.

Friday the sixteenth. President Trump signs an executive order implementing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act — and uses it to waive the Russia provisions that were about to take effect on the eighteenth.
Wait. He signs the law and then waives the law?
He signed the Act in September. The Senate passed it eighty-six to eleven. The order waives thirteen of its sections.
[scoffs] For how long?
That's the detail. The waivers, quote, shall remain in effect until such time as the President or the Secretary of State decides otherwise. No sunset. No review date.
So indefinitely.
Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who voted for it, asked: what part of enforcing a law passed eighty-six to eleven by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?
And the Hormuz link?
Tillis again. If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he said, he can do it by solving the Iran problem.
[deadpan] Money block. Claire, the inflation number this week made no sense to me.
It made no sense to the bond market either, and that's the story. American consumer prices rose zero point six per cent in September. Annual rate three point seven.
Driven by what?
Energy. Up five point two per cent on the month, twenty point four on the year. Gasoline up thirty-four point two per cent year on year.
That's Hormuz arriving in an American supermarket.
Exactly that. Now — a hot inflation print in a hiking cycle should push yields up.
And they went?
Down. The ten-year fell fifteen basis points to five point zero nine. The thirty-year fell seventeen. The two-year only six.
[curious] Why does that pattern matter?
Because the long end falling faster than the short end is called a bull flattening, and it doesn't mean rate cuts. It means the market thinks growth is about to be destroyed.
Destroyed by what?
The AI trade cracked. Twenty of the largest AI and semiconductor names shed more than a trillion dollars in the week. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell for an eighth straight session.
So the inflation is real, but the growth scare is bigger.

That's the week in one sentence. And the cross-asset check backs it. Volatility up twenty-one per cent, Nasdaq down four and a half, but the Dow up zero point seven — that's rotation, not panic. The dollar fell, so it isn't a dollar-bid risk-off. Gold was flat, which argues against inflation panic.
And Singapore?
The Monetary Authority held on the fourteenth. No change to the band's slope, width or centre, after tightening in April and July.
Held, with third-quarter growth at what?
Five point four per cent year on year. And it warned that the risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside, naming energy.
So it's absorbing the shock rather than leaning against it.
The currency barely moved, and the Straits Times index rose a quarter per cent in a week the Nasdaq fell four and a half.
[warmly] The defensive index doing its job.
Our local story is the haze, and it's the keystone of the whole issue.
How bad was it?
Friday's peak was two hundred and twenty-nine, the highest reading of the year. Sunday's forecast is a hundred and fifty to two hundred and twenty.
And the enforcement? We reported the notices last issue.

Seven Indonesian companies, the first ever issued under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. Here's what's new. The agency confirmed this week that the investigations it opened in two thousand and fifteen, into four companies, are still open.
[pause] Eleven years.
Eleven years, no prosecution, no penalty. And the minister didn't oversell it. She said: it is not easy, I will be the first to admit, but we must try — and then, even if it may not be so effective.
That's unusually honest for an enforcement announcement.

The sentence that gives the issue its spine is buried in the agency's own bulletin, though. Explaining why it can't say how much is burning, it wrote: the full extent of the hotspot and smoke haze situation could not be determined due to extensive cloud cover.
[drawn out] The satellites that would count the fires can't see through the smoke the fires make.
That's the issue, Theo. That's the whole issue.
Technology — and this one has the same shape.
China's commerce ministry proposed export controls on forty technologies on the sixteenth. Twenty-three of them artificial intelligence.
Chips?
Models. Large models, agents, computing clusters. But read the exclusion: technologies already in the public domain through open-source release or academic publication fall outside it entirely.
[amused] So if you publish your weights, you escape the export regime.
A regime with a door in it, and the door is the part everyone uses. Alibaba's Qwen family alone draws about a hundred and forty-one million downloads.
What did the self-hosting crowd make of that?
They read the carve-out as a threat, not a reassurance. The worry is it chills future Chinese open-weight releases even as it exempts the past ones.
Speaking of which — the home lab number this week is wild.
Nvidia released Nemotron Bolt. Seventy-four billion parameters, compressed to fit in twenty-four gigabytes.
[gasps] Seventy-four billion on one card?
Most of the weights carried at just over two bits each. It runs at about eighty-four tokens a second.
That sounds like a win.

Here's the honest part, and Nvidia published it themselves. On the same benchmark, Qwen runs at ninety-seven tokens a second and Gemma at a hundred. Both faster. On an agent replay, Bolt is slower. Smaller models beat it on three of its own accuracy rows.
So two bits buys you fit, not speed.
Fit, and nothing else. The vendor's second table says so for anyone who scrolls.
And the opposite case?

Reflection released Beam one point zero under Apache two — five hundred and one billion parameters, genuinely open. But the quantisation ladder tells you what that costs: four-bit weights are about two hundred and eighty-six gibibytes.
Which means?
A licence you can read is not a model you can run.
[laughs] That's going on a sticker. Okay — the gadget.
Amazon launched the Bee Frontier on the fifteenth. A wristband that listens all day. Seventy-four dollars ninety-nine, seven days of battery, and a subscription at eleven ninety-nine a month.
Singapore price?
None. US only at launch. And as of yesterday there is no full independent review of it anywhere.
For a device whose whole job is recording conversations.
A former senior principal security engineer at Amazon's own cloud arm, Jeff Williams, puts the objection best. He says Bee is asking the wrong person for permission.
[thoughtful] Because the consent prompt appears on the wearer's phone.

And nothing enforces it. The indicator light disappears under a sleeve. He calls the design a liability allocation that shifts responsibility onto the wearer — while the privacy protections cover the wearer, not the bystander whose words land in a transcript they can't see, access or delete.
And under our own data law that's a live question, not an academic one.
Right. Take my hand, Theo — actually, no. That's your line.
[laughs] Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
Carnivorous plants. And I did not expect the mechanism to be this good.
A Nepenthes pitcher doesn't trap anything. It makes a surface that stops working.
Explain that.

The rim — the peristome — is completely wettable. Rain spreads across it as an unbroken film instead of beading. That film defeats the sticky pads on an insect's feet, and the rim's ridges grip in one direction only.
So the ant can walk up but not stand still.
Bohn and Federle measured it in two thousand and four. On a dry rim, one ant species fell in on none of thirty-seven visits. Weaver ants, none of eighteen.
And wet?
Fourteen out of fourteen. And twenty-one out of twenty-one.
[gasps] Every single one. Both species.
The plant isn't catching insects. It's waiting for rain.
And this grows here?

Three species grow wild in Singapore. The commonest is least concern and tolerates pollution. Two others are vulnerable — Kent Ridge Park, the catchment forests, and one of them on the coastal cliffs of the Southern Islands, growing down to the tide line.
Can you go and look?
Look, don't touch. Under the Parks and Trees Act, collecting any part of a plant in a reserve carries a fine up to fifty thousand dollars, six months, or both.
[exhales] For a pitcher.

For a pitcher. Now the gear, because this is where it got interesting. The grail of this hobby was Nepenthes rajah — the species whose collection pressure put the whole genus under international trade control.
What does a grail cost?
Twenty euros.
[laughs] Twenty?
Twenty, from a German lab. Tissue culture collapsed the entire grail tier. What the market prices now isn't rarity, it's provenance — a named clone, a wild locality.
So what is expensive?

The refrigerator. Lowland species grow outdoors here essentially free — the whole windowsill setup is maybe a hundred and twenty to two hundred dollars. But the highland species want a ten to fifteen degree night drop.
In Singapore. Holding fifteen degrees against thirty.
With a compressor that barely stops. Six hundred to twelve hundred dollars a year, and nobody budgets it.
And the sceptic?

The sceptic is the best thing on the desk. That night-drop orthodoxy — the thing the entire equipment tier rests on — has never been tested. Someone asked on a British forum in two thousand and eight whether there was any study on how long temperatures need to drop.
And?
Nobody answered. Eighteen years later, nobody has.
[deadpan] An industry built on an unanswered forum post.
There's also no published survival rate anywhere in the hobby. Lots of acquisition posts, lots of death threads, no denominator.
Culture and the body — quickly, what else is worth knowing?
The Atelier took sewing machines, and found a real story. Bernina decided on the eighteenth of February to move its last Swiss production to Thailand. Twenty-seven redundancies in Steckborn.
And the marketing?
Its Singapore site still reads: Swiss tradition and perfection since eighteen ninety-three. I checked that myself yesterday.
[wry] Development stays Swiss, assembly doesn't.

And the broader lesson is that almost nothing about a sewing machine is legible from the badge. Singer's own About page contains not one word about manufacturing. Pfaff dot com is now a four-line redirect into the Singer webstore.
The eighteen sixty-two German marque.
A product tab. Meanwhile the real industrial Pfaff is a separate Chinese-owned company that still makes machines.
Fitness?

A review of two hundred and eighty-four trials, eighteen thousand seven hundred and fifty adults. The best single intervention for systolic blood pressure was aquatic exercise — ten point three millimetres of mercury.
Swimming. Not the gym.
Swimming. Though read the dose section carefully — the headline optima are points on a fitted curve, not doses anyone was actually randomised to receive.
And this week, outdoors is off anyway.
At these readings, train indoors. Judge it on the one-hour particulate number, not the daily headline.
Travel — and the Nara piece changed my mind about something.
The city published its own visitor survey in July. Sixteen point one million visitors last year. Only thirteen point nine per cent stayed the night.
Six in seven just pass through.
And the case against that isn't the money. It's the opening hours. Almost everything in Nara happens before eight in the morning or after five in the evening.
So the day-tripper gets?

The Great Buddha Hall, which shuts at half past five and charges eight hundred yen. Meanwhile, two hundred metres up the hill, the Nigatsu-dō is a National Treasure, free, and open twenty-four hours a day.
[pause] Everyone queues for the one that closes.
Everyone queues for the one that closes.
Give me the deer fact. I know there's a deer fact.
The foundation counted the herd in July. One thousand six hundred and eighty-seven — a record, up two hundred and twenty-two in a year.
And the crackers? People always ask about the crackers.
Rice bran, wheat flour and water. Nothing else — no sugar, no flavouring, because the deer eat them every day. Two hundred yen for ten.
[amused] And the paper band?
Even the paper and the glue are chosen so they do the deer no harm if eaten.
[laughs] That's wonderful. And the injuries everyone warns about?
Seventy-one people hurt in one financial year. None hospitalised. Not one. Fifty of them — seventy per cent — got disinfection and a plaster.
So they're a nuisance, not a danger.
A reliable nuisance to anyone holding a cracker and hesitating.
[thoughtful] And the long read.
Indonesia. There's a word there — Rojali. It's an ordinary man's name, and also an acronym meaning, roughly, the group that rarely buys.
Meaning what?
Indonesian malls are as full as they have ever been, and the tills aren't moving. People come to eat, to cool off, to walk, and they leave.
Is that just a joke, or is it in the data?

It's in two sets of data that disagree. Bank Indonesia says real retail sales grew one point three per cent in August. The statistics agency says real household consumption grew five point zero six in the second quarter.
Both official.
Both official. The gap is about four percentage points of an economy, and that gap is where the word lives.
Why are people doing it?

Because it's rational. On an average wage of three point two nine million rupiah a month, the marginal mall visit costs nothing and delivers air conditioning, a toilet, light, security and somewhere to be. The marginal purchase is cheaper online.
So the mall became a public space.
It became the only free, cool, safe public space most Indonesian cities offer. A survey found that of eleven reasons people gave for going, only three had anything to do with shopping.
And the argument underneath?
The middle class shrank. Fifty-nine and a half million in twenty eighteen, forty-seven point nine million in twenty twenty-four.
It went backwards. Before the country got rich.

And the growth rate held up anyway, because somebody else started spending. Government consumption grew nearly sixteen per cent year on year against households' five. The household share of the economy fell to fifty-three point three per cent.
[drawn out] So consumption got nationalised.
That's the argument. The state became the buyer the mall lost.
Is there a counter-case?
A good one. The mall owners say it's a Jakarta story projected nationally, and a cycle. Consumer confidence is high. And the middle class actually led spending in the last festive season.
So what would prove it wrong?
Two consecutive quarters of retail sales above four per cent. That's the kill switch, and we've logged it.
[warmly] What struck me reading the whole issue is how often the honest answer was: we don't know, and here's who couldn't count it.
A monitoring centre that can't count attacks. Satellites that can't see through smoke. A ledger four months late. A hobby with no survival rate.
And then Nara, where somebody walks the park every July and writes the number down.
That's the difference between a fact and a rumour. Usually just an institution that kept a list.
[exhales] That's the Briefing, then.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
